en: The euro: a single currency for Europe Christian Noyer, Conference Organized by IPAG School "The euro: a single currency for Europe", Paris, 1 October 1998 Introduction Three months now separate us from the beginning of its third phase of economic and monetary union. On January 1, 1999, the euro will become the only currency of the eleven countries that are initially participating. For Europe and for the rest of the world, the single currency project is a capital. The euro is the opportunity to establish truly and permanently in Europe's market for price stability, which is the central source of the european currency and the central currency of the Union's steel industry. I would also like to briefly describe the monetary policy instruments of the European Central Bank and inform you of the current work on the implementation of the monetary policy strategy. The European Central Bank will contribute to the development of a common culture of stability, which must also be the main determinant of fiscal and change policies. The European Central Bank will contribute to the development of a single culture of stability? European and national institutions have been preparing the single currency for several years. Among them, the European Central Bank will contribute to the development of a single currency. The objective of price stability is the necessary condition for a strong and balanced economic development. I would just like to mention two major reasons. There is first the best content in price information. Prices, when stable, can better inform economic agents about the quality of products, goods or services, which enables us to improve the relevance of decision making and thus the optimal allocation of resources. Then there is the fact that the reduction of the uncertainty about future developments of the prices makes evidence of the quality of products, goods or services more likely to improve the relevance of decision-making and thus the optimal allocation of resources. After that, there is the fact that the reduction of the future evolution of the prices makes it more likely to be considered as a long-term price for the price of products, goods or services. Inflation leads to redistributions of wealth that are not democratically eradicated, and that still harmonise the most fragile categories of the population. The banking systems and financial markets of the participating countries must also be solid and stable in order to ensure the financing of the economies and to enable effective and rapid transmission of monetary policy. The driving systems in this area are now well harmonised at European Union level, based on European directives. The European Central Bank of Europe, and before they are implemented in the various institutions of the euro area, is responsible for the financing of the economy and for the efficient and rapid transmission of monetary policy. This culture of stability must also be part of the main determinant of fiscal, economic and change policies The economies of the euro area will not be able to cope fully unless, outside the stability of prices, several other unnecessary conditions are met. These conditions affect three areas: fiscal policies, economic policies and change policy. Budgetary policies must reduce public debt and reduce or cancel public deficits. In this regard, the Stability and Growth Pact, on which the European Council does not establish the principles of justice and the rule of law, is based on the principle of justice. The other aspects of economic policies must as far as they are concerned to promote certain elections or other neutral ones by their relationship. I would like to quote two of these elections among the most important ones in order to promote sustainable and balanced growth. On the one hand, goods and labour markets must remain or become sufficiently flexible. On the other hand, wage policies must remain modern, which means taking full account of the realisation of their price stability objective. The objectives of the European Central Bank are clearly clear and fully guaranteed. For the most effective purpose, the European Central Bank must be transparent and responsible. The objectives of the European Central Bank are clear and independent. The European Central Bank is clearly defined and its independence is guaranteed. The Governing Council of the European Central Bank includes the President, the Vice-President and the other four members of the Director of the ECB, as well as the Governors of the national central banks of the participating countries, 17 persons. The members of the Governing Council may not receive or apply for advice from national governments, national institutions, the European Commission or other European institutions. To be as effective as possible, the European Central Bank must be transparent and responsible for its independence as required by the European Central Bank of major duties, in terms of transparency and of what is called the United Kingdom of Great Britain. The Maastricht Treaty also states that the European Central Bank must report an annual report to the European Parliament, the European Commission, the Council of Ministers and the European Council, which should describe the monetary policy conducted during its school year and the strategy adopted as well as the guidelines held for the current year. The Treaty provides that the European Parliament will hold an annual debate on this report and that the President and the members of the European Central Bank are responsible for the issues of the European Parliament and the Council.
